title: The Before Survey
dek: A 27 March 2026 peace-agreement survey found a briar-sealed sinkhole, Delerium haze, worked stone, shattered remains, and an underground swarm beneath The Before.

body:
The modern survey of The Before is public campaign history even though the ruins’ ancient origin remains protected. On 27 March 2026, Pristinian adventurers wait outside town for a Rahuvian scholarly delegation. The expedition is an obligation of the peace agreement that ended the war, making historical investigation part of diplomacy rather than private treasure hunting.

Evidence boundary: this record describes what the expedition observed in 2026. It does not publicly disclose who built the ruins, what destroyed them, or the protected history beneath their contamination.

A feared place before it was an expedition

On 8 June 2024, a strange signal from The Before pierced the air. Long-time Pristinia residents recognized it immediately, reacting with hope, fear, and reluctance to say what it might mean. The adventurers were not discovering a brand-new dungeon; they were entering a place the local population already remembered.

Later testimony weakened every simple theory of ownership. Arjahn remembered a wizard warning that he did not control everything in the ruins, naming an Aboleth as one example, and recalled a gargantuan metal creature within the caves. The warning itself may not be wholly trustworthy, but repeated expeditions support the narrower conclusion: no recovered faction can be assumed to control every system, creature, or passage in The Before.

A ruin that changes between visits

Repeated expeditions turned scattered fear into accumulated preparation. Signals could be imitated, creatures could escape with information, caves could collapse, and contamination could persist. By 2026 the best-known entrance had physically changed behind a dense barrier of faintly glowing briars. Player knowledge grew without converting the site into conquered territory.

The survey company

Thorn, Camilla, Lady Severina, Saoirse, Miri and the Rahuvian scholars, and other companions approach together. Thorn leads once the delegation arrives. The scholars remain tightly grouped, recording evidence while the adventurers manage threats.

A sealed approach

The best-known entrance has changed. Thick briars surround it, cracks in their stems emit a faint purple glow, and Thorn identifies the smell as Delerium. Burning the barrier replaces it with low purple mist. Wind magic can clear only a temporary space, and the haze flows into an eighty-foot sinkhole descending to the cavern.

Worked stone under the earth

Below, a northern passage of cracked carved stone opens into a larger chamber. The party observes a ruined fountain, a broken archway, side caverns, humanoid skeletons, and an anguished outstretched statue. The placement of the remains suggests people once ran from something. When approached, the statue collapses into fine purple-hued dust.

The western cavern

A growing buzz from the silent western passage becomes hundreds of stirges. The party protects the scholars and retreats to the first cavern, where the delegation raises a fabric barrier and prepares to camp. The quest ends with the survey incomplete: evidence has been secured, but the northern ruins, eastern glow, western threat, and contamination mechanism remain unresolved.

What became true

The peace agreement now has material consequences: Rahuvian scholars are physically present in Prima, a known entrance to The Before has changed, and a formal survey has begun. The ruins are not a static historical footnote. Their hazards continue to alter, spread, and demand joint investigation.

Current state and open questions

The survey remains incomplete. Who built the oldest systems, whether the Rahu ever exercised complete control, which inhabitants are native or deliberately placed, why the entrance changed, and what other passages remain undiscovered are all open. The public record preserves what modern expeditions observed; the protected vault holds the ancient history that player characters should not automatically know.

18 September · when following the call costs too much

Shared dreams bring another company to the ruins. A moving tree reveals an entrance, but the descent leads into heavy haze. Vessalia becomes contaminated and turns back with the unwell Pell. Di’trillio continues and later returns to find his companions. Exploration deepens their exposure without making the ruins safe or resolving their ancient history. Follow this later expedition.

Scene sources: 1, 2, 3, 4.

March 2024 · two ways of taking notes

Scribonia seeks Jako’s experience with natural environments before exploring the ruins. Jako agrees that traveling together offers mutual protection. Along the way, Scribonia catalogs plants and animals and gathers samples; Jako records them in drawings. They exchange explanations of words and childhood customs. The expedition makes room for patient observation and teaching, not only combat or the search for treasure.

Scene evidence: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

September 2026 · old notes guide a new expedition

Minerva briefs later explorers to move quietly, watch for aberrations and avoid entering or casting inside the haze. She explicitly cites Scribonia’s notes for the warning that it feeds on spells. She asks the group to report historically interesting finds to her. The briefing establishes inherited precautions and an ongoing research interest; it does not resolve the ruins’ origins or independently prove every hazard rule she repeats.

Scene evidence: 1.

December 2025 · a traveler’s unfinished warnings

Greg’s work-in-progress notes, posted on 12 December 2025, records uncertainty over whether the terrain changes or his senses are being confused. He suggests water can help locate a monster and attributes a warning about extremely dangerous clicking sounds to Reuben.

These are remembered field heuristics and a named warning, not reliable detection rules or a completed explanation of the ruins. The note preserves what travelers thought worth passing on before the later survey; it neither resolves the site’s protected ancient history nor establishes who controlled it.
